title: The War of Art
author: Steven Pressfield
summary:
The War of Art gives a name to the force that appears whenever a person tries to begin meaningful work: Resistance. Resistance takes many forms—procrastination, distraction, perfectionism, self-doubt, drama, endless preparation, and the belief that one must first feel inspired. Pressfield argues that Resistance is strongest around the work that matters most.

The book contrasts the amateur and the professional. The amateur waits for mood, approval, confidence, and ideal conditions. The professional shows up according to a standard. This does not mean becoming cold or joyless. It means treating one’s calling with enough respect to work even when enthusiasm is absent.

For interns, the book is powerful because early careers are full of uncertainty. Many people postpone difficult applications, writing, exercise, or creative work because they interpret discomfort as a sign to stop. Pressfield reframes discomfort as evidence that the work may be important. The practical lesson is simple but demanding: sit down, begin, and keep returning. Courage often appears after the work has started, not before.
